title: Arjan and Hargobind
hookLine: then Guru Arjan and Guru Hargobind
last: AMAR DAS — AMAR DAS, RAM DAS.

lines: HIS SON IS STILL A BOY.
TWO SWORDS, AND A RAISED SEAT.
cards: Lahore. A man is held by the authorities and dies after being tortured. Sikh tradition remembers him sitting calm through it, saying God's will is sweet.
He is the Guru, and his son is still a boy. What does a boy do with that? This one, tradition says, put on two swords.
Then he built a raised platform facing the Harmandir Sahib. The father had built a house for the scripture. The son built a seat for the community's courage.

teach.h: ARJAN: THE HOUSE AND THE BOOK.
teach.b: The Ardas line goes: arjan hargobind no simrau. Remember Arjan and Hargobind. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was the son of Guru Ram Das.
He finished the pool at Amritsar and built the Harmandir Sahib in its middle, with doors on all four sides, open to everyone from every direction.
He compiled the Adi Granth, gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, his own, and the hymns of saints from other backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim, and installed it in the Harmandir.
He wrote the Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, which we read earlier this year. And he was executed in Lahore under the emperor Jahangir.

teach.h: REMEMBERED AS THE FIRST SIKH MARTYR.
teach.b: Sikhs remember him as the first Sikh martyr. Tradition remembers him living out a line of his own bani, which Sikhs often say as tera bhana meetha laage: Your will is sweet. Guru Hargobind, his son, became Guru as a boy.
Tradition says he wore two swords, one called miri, for worldly responsibility, and one called piri, for the spiritual.
And he built the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, facing the Harmandir: a seat of community authority beside the house of prayer.
Later he was held in Gwalior fort; Sikhs remember his release, along with fifty-two imprisoned princes, on Bandi Chhor Divas, which falls with Diwali.
The father built the house and the book, and gave his life quietly. The son added the sword and the throne, so the community could stand.
The Ardas holds both in one breath: the calm and the courage, the scripture and the seat.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Arjan and Guru Hargobind; Guru Arjan's martyrdom is marked each year, often with chhabeels serving cold drinks to passersby, and Bandi Chhor Divas recalls Guru Hargobind's release.

o: worldly and spiritual authority, the two swords
the two halves of the Harmandir's doors
the names of Guru Arjan's two sons

games.q: Arjan and Hargobind — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Arjan is remembered as the first Sikh martyr
he was executed in Lahore under the emperor Jahangir.
the Adi Granth contains only the Gurus' hymns
Guru Arjan included saints from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds too.
Guru Hargobind's two swords stand for miri and piri
worldly responsibility and the spiritual, side by side.

games.q: you're still a boy, and your father, the Guru, has just been killed in Lahore. tradition says you become Guru. what do you do?
o: put on two swords and build the Akal Takht.
games.why: tradition says Guru Hargobind wore miri and piri and built the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir, so the community could stand.

practice: Hands open on your knees, on a long out-breath, say Arjan, calm like four open doors; then sit a little taller, close your hands gently, and say Hargobind, steady like someone standing up straight.
If you pray, say tera bhana meetha laage, Your will is sweet, after them; if you don't, think about where you need calm today, and where you need courage.

wordCard.voice: Miri piri, worldly and spiritual authority. Guru Hargobind wore the two swords, miri and piri, after his father Guru Arjan, the first Sikh martyr, built the house and the book.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: miri piri, worldly and spiritual authority, the two swords of Guru Hargobind.

carryVoice: Your line: arjan, hargobind. The calm and the courage, held in one breath. Until tomorrow.
